1.summary: Why knowing SQL is not the whole story: what a DBMS adds on top of storage, why data is not yet information, and why only data that satisfies the right constraints represents reality.

facts.d: Data definitions (models, types), efficient storage and processing, integrity rules and constraints, reliability and durability, controlled access, multiuser cooperation, data security and audit.
Developer surveys put PostgreSQL, SQLite and MySQL at the top, and relational DBMSs hold roughly three quarters of the market share shown on the slide.
Elementary, independent, low redundancy, easy to store, manipulate and compress, and meaningless without interpretation.
Interpreted data. The interpretation depends on syntax and semantics; information is redundant, complex and difficult to process. Information = data plus interpretation.
Reality is described by a model; the database stores data plus rules (constraints); the DBMS adds storage, management, access control and multiuser work.
Of all structurally representable states, only the admissible ones (those that satisfy the declared constraints) can stand for reality.

Syntactic validity: the value has an allowed type or format (age is an integer). Structural integrity: keys and references satisfy schema rules (the referenced car exists). Semantic integrity: the state obeys business rules (kids cannot drive a car).
The same CARS, PEOPLE and CAR_PERSON tables can describe car rentals, delivery vehicles, a car dealer's stock or fatal accidents; each reality needs different constraints.
Distinguish the database from the DBMS, and data from information: storing information needs both data and rules (constraints).

traps: Database vs DBMS: the database is the stored data and rules; the DBMS is the software that stores, manages and controls access to it.
A value of the right type can still be invalid: syntactic validity says nothing about references (structural) or business rules (semantic).
The schema alone does not tell you which reality it describes; the constraints do.

2.summary: The relational model's building blocks and properties, relational algebra from selection to division, transformation rules used by optimisers, and where SQL departs from the model: duplicates, order and NULLs with three-valued logic.

facts.d: A domain is a set of possible values (not necessarily a simple type); a relation is a subset of a Cartesian product of domains; a tuple is one element of the relation; an attribute is one element of the tuple. The active domain is the set of values currently present.
Relations and attributes are identified by name; domains hold atomic values and there is no NULL; no two tuples are the same; the order of tuples and of attributes is irrelevant.
Not every Cartesian product represents valid information; domain constraints check single attributes but cannot guarantee data integrity.
Operators take relations and return a relation with all relation properties; an expression describes a transformation, not an implementation; operations can be chained.

Selection σ filters tuples by a predicate; projection π keeps listed attributes and eliminates duplicates; union ∪ and difference \ need compatible relations; Cartesian product × needs distinct attribute names; rename ρ fixes names.
Intersection R ∩ S = R \ (R \ S). Theta join R ⨝θ S = σθ(R × S). Equi join uses equality conditions. Natural join is an equi join on all same-named attributes, keeping one copy of each.
R ⋉ S = π attr(R) (R ⨝ S): tuples of R that have a partner. R ⩥ S = R \ (R ⋉ S): tuples without one. R ÷ S = πX(R) \ πX((πX(R) × S) \ R) for attr(R) = X ∪ Y and attr(S) = Y.
Selections commute and combine; push selections below joins to cut tuples early; projections cascade (πX(πY(R)) = πX(R) iff X ⊆ Y) and can be pushed down; natural join is commutative and associative.
SQL keeps duplicates unless DISTINCT, UNION, EXCEPT remove them (UNION ALL, EXCEPT ALL keep them); rows have an order (ORDER BY, GROUP BY, indexes); SQL has NULLs and outer joins.
Comparisons with NULL give UNKNOWN. FALSE AND anything = FALSE; TRUE OR anything = TRUE; NOT UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN; UNKNOWN AND TRUE = UNKNOWN; UNKNOWN OR FALSE = UNKNOWN.

facts.t: A WHERE clause that is not always true
facts.d: WHERE CourseCode > 300 OR NOT (CourseCode > 300) skips rows where CourseCode is NULL, because UNKNOWN OR UNKNOWN is UNKNOWN; the same condition on a non-NULL column returns every row.

formulas.name: Intersection from difference
formulas.expr: R ∩ S = R \ (R \ S) = S \ (S \ R)

formulas.name: Division
formulas.expr: R ÷ S = πX(R) \ πX( (πX(R) × S) \ R )

traps: Projection removes duplicates in the model; SELECT without DISTINCT does not.
Selection after projection fails when the predicate uses an attribute the projection dropped (σSSN<1000 over πFName,LName).
Cartesian product needs distinct attribute names; πSSN,FName × πSSN,LName needs a rename first.
NULL = NULL is UNKNOWN, not TRUE; EXCEPT and NOT EXISTS can return different rows when NULLs appear.

3.summary: Why one big table repeats facts and causes anomalies, how decomposition splits it into facts, what makes a decomposition good (lossless, dependency preserving), and the theory of functional dependencies with Armstrong's axioms.

facts.d: In U(SSN, FName, LName, CourseCode, CourseName, FinalGrade) the same person and the same course are stored again in every row that mentions them.

Storing several independent facts in one relation wastes space and causes update, insert and delete anomalies; domain constraints (type, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK) cannot keep repeated facts consistent.

U splits into R1 = πSSN,FName,LName(U) (people), R2 = πCourseCode,CourseName(U) (courses) and R3 = πSSN,CourseCode,FinalGrade(U) (grades). A decomposition that removes the anomalies is called normalisation.
Decomposing R(XY) into R1 = πX(R) and R2 = πY(R) must be lossless (R1 ⨝ R2 = R) and, if possible, functional dependency preserving.
R(ABC) with tuples (a1,b1,c1) and (a2,b2,c1) split into R1(AC), R2(BC) joins back into four tuples: two of them are spurious, so information is lost.
X → Y holds iff any two tuples that agree on X also agree on Y. FDs are inferred from the description of reality, not from the current content, and hold even in an empty relation.
Identifying facts (sets of attributes), finding candidate and primary keys, and defining normal forms and normalisation.
Its name, its set of attributes and the set of FDs that hold in it, e.g. R(ABCDE, A → BC, C → D, DA → E).
X → Y is trivial if Y ⊆ X, non-trivial if Y ⊈ X, and completely non-trivial if X ∩ Y = ∅. SSN, CourseCode → SSN is trivial; SSN, CourseCode → SSN, FinalGrade is non-trivial but not completely.
Transitivity: X → Y and Y → Z give X → Z. Augmentation: X → Y gives XZ → YZ. Reflexivity: Y ⊆ X gives X → Y. Derived: union, decomposition and pseudotransitivity.

formulas.name: Pseudotransitivity
formulas.expr: X → Y and YW → Z  ⇒  XW → Z

traps: A FD cannot be proven from sample rows; rows can only refute it. FDs come from the description of reality.
Lossless join is about getting R back exactly; the join of a lossy decomposition has more tuples, not fewer.
Union and decomposition are derived rules, not among the three basic axioms (transitivity, augmentation, reflexivity).

4.summary: The tools of normalisation: closures of FD sets and attribute sets, superkeys and candidate keys, prime attributes, the normal forms from 1NF to BCNF, minimal covers, iterative decomposition and 3NF synthesis.

facts.t: Closure of a set of FDs
facts.d: F+ contains every FD in F plus every FD that follows from them by Armstrong's axioms.
A decomposition of R(XY, F) into R1(X, F1) and R2(Y, F2) where both are in the desired normal form, the join is lossless, and if possible F+ = (F1 ∪ F2)+.
X+ is every attribute functionally dependent on X under F. Properties: extensivity (X ⊆ X+), monotonicity (X ⊆ Y ⇒ X+ ⊆ Y+), idempotence ((X+)+ = X+).
Start with result = X; repeat over all FDs Y → Z and add Z whenever Y ⊆ result; stop when a full pass adds nothing.
X → Y holds iff Y ⊆ X+. Z is a superkey iff Z+ is all attributes. A candidate key is a minimal superkey. Normal-form tests refer to the candidate keys.
Z is a candidate key if Z+ = X and removing any single attribute z1 gives (Z \ z1)+ ≠ X.

1. Take the mandatory attributes, those on no right-hand side. 2. If their closure is everything, that is the only key. 3. Otherwise add combinations of the rest, 4. check closure and minimality, 5. prune supersets of keys already found.
A prime attribute belongs to at least one candidate key; a non-prime attribute belongs to none.

1NF: atomic values. 2NF: 1NF and every non-prime attribute is fully dependent on every candidate key. 3NF: 2NF and for every non-trivial X → Y in F+, X is a superkey or Y is prime. BCNF: 3NF and X is always a superkey.

With Student, Course → Instructor and Instructor → Course the keys are {Student, Course} and {Student, Instructor}; every attribute is prime, so it is 3NF, but Instructor → Course has a non-key left side, so it is not BCNF.

G is a minimal cover of F if G+ = F+, every FD has one attribute on the right, no left side has extraneous attributes, and no FD can be removed. Steps: split right sides, remove extraneous left attributes, remove redundant FDs.

Find keys, decide the NF and the FDs that violate the next one, pick one X → Y, split into R1(XY) and R2(XZ) (everything except Y), project F+ onto both and repeat. Each step is lossless; the slide notes FDs are preserved up to 3NF.

Minimal cover, group FDs with the same left side, one relation per group, drop relations contained in others, and add a relation holding a candidate key if none has one. The result is lossless, dependency preserving and in 3NF.

formulas.name: Superkey
formulas.expr: Z is a superkey of R(X, F)  ⇔  Z+ = X

formulas.name: Binary lossless test
formulas.expr: (X ∩ Y) → X ∈ F+  or  (X ∩ Y) → Y ∈ F+

formulas.name: Example closure
formulas.expr: R(ABCDE, A → BC, C → D, DA → E):  A+ = ABCDE,  C+ = CD

traps: The common-attribute test (X ∩ Y) → X or (X ∩ Y) → Y decides whether a binary decomposition is lossless; slide 13 prints it next to dependency preservation, which is checked with F+ = (F1 ∪ F2)+.
3NF lets X → Y with a non-superkey X only when Y is prime; BCNF never does.
A relation whose candidate keys are all single attributes is automatically in 2NF; it can still fail 3NF (A → B → C).
In the slide 23 example AC → E is redundant: A → B and BC → E already imply it, so the minimal cover is A → B, C → D, BC → E, DE → C.

5.summary: Worked normalisation of R(ABCDE, A → B, C → D, BC → DE, DE → C, AC → D) by 3NF synthesis and by the iterative procedure, a comparison of the two results, and handy shortcuts for deciding normal forms.

facts.d: R(ABCDE, A → B, C → D, BC → DE, DE → C, AC → D) reduces to the minimal cover A → B, C → D, BC → E, DE → C.

facts.t: Step 2: one relation per FD group
facts.d: R1(AB, A → B), R2(CD, C → D), R3(BCE, BC → E), R4(CDE, DE → C, C → D); R2 is contained in R4 and is dropped.
The candidate keys of R are AC and ADE. No relation contains one, so R5(AC) is added: the 3NF result is R1(AB), R3(BCE), R4(CDE), R5(AC).
A table of which FD (left and right side) fits inside which relation shows every FD of the minimal cover lives in some relation.
To go further, decide each relation's NF, find an FD that violates the next NF, and use it for a binary decomposition.
Synthesis gives R1(AB) BCNF, R3(BCE) BCNF, R4(CDE) 3NF, R5(AC) BCNF. The iterative procedure gives R1(AB), R2(CD) and R3(ACE, AC → E), all BCNF, but DE → C no longer fits in any relation.
For a relation in 1NF: all keys single-attribute ⇒ 2NF; all attributes prime ⇒ 3NF; exactly one key and 3NF ⇒ BCNF; a non-prime attribute partially dependent on a key ⇒ not 2NF.

formulas.name: Minimal cover of the example
formulas.expr: A → B, C → D, BC → E, DE → C

traps: R4(CDE, DE → C, C → D) is 3NF but not BCNF: its keys are DE and CE, so C → D has a non-key left side, yet D is prime.
Synthesis keeps every dependency; reaching BCNF by decomposition may lose one (here DE → C).

questions.q: Besides storing tables, what does a database management system provide? Name at least five services.
questions.a:
- Data definitions: data models and types
- Efficient storage and processing
- Integrity rules and constraints
- Reliability and durability
- Controlled access
- Multiuser cooperation
- Data security and audit
questions.hint: Think about what can go wrong when many users and programs share data for years.

questions.q: Explain the difference between data and information, giving two properties of each.
questions.a:
Data is elementary, independent and low in redundancy; it is easy to store, manipulate and compress, but meaningless without interpretation.
Information is interpreted data: its meaning depends on syntax and semantics, and it is redundant, complex and hard to process.
Information = data plus interpretation.
questions.hint: The finger-counting example: the same gesture, different numbers.

questions.q: Name the three levels of data validity from the lecture and give an example of a violation of each.
questions.a:
- Syntactic validity: the value has an allowed type or format. Violation: an age stored as text.
- Structural integrity: keys and references satisfy the schema. Violation: a rental refers to a car that does not exist.
- Semantic integrity: the state obeys business rules. Violation: a child registered as the driver of a car.
questions.hint: Type, references, business rules.

questions.q: The tables CARS(VIN, …), PEOPLE(SSN, …) and CAR_PERSON(VIN, SSN, Date) can describe car rentals or fatal accidents. Why does the same schema need different constraints, and give one constraint that differs?
questions.a:
A schema only fixes structure; which states are admissible depends on the reality it models.
For rentals, one car can be linked to many people over time but to one person on a given date, and the person needs a driving licence.
For fatal accidents, each person appears at most once in CAR_PERSON (a person dies once), while a car can be linked to several victims of the same accident.
questions.hint: What can happen at most once in each scenario?

questions.q: A database records a nine-year-old as the driver in a car rental. Which level of validity is violated?
questions.hint: Every value has the right type and every reference exists.
questions.r: Slide 14: the age is a valid integer and the referenced person and car exist, so syntax and structure are fine. The state breaks a business rule (children cannot drive), which is semantic integrity.

questions.q: According to the lecture, which property belongs to data rather than to information?
o: Low redundancy and easy to compress
Redundant, complex and hard to process
questions.hint: One side is raw and simple, the other interpreted and rich.
questions.r: Slide 11: data is elementary, independent, low in redundancy and easy to store and compress, but meaningless without interpretation. Interpretation, redundancy and complexity describe information.

questions.q: Which states of a database can represent reality?
o: Only admissible states that satisfy the declared constraints
Every state the table structure can physically represent
Only states that were inserted through a transaction
Any state that uses the correct data types for every column
questions.hint: Slide 13 draws a smaller region inside all representable states.
questions.r: Slide 13: among all structurally representable states, only the admissible ones, those satisfying the declared constraints, can stand for reality. Correct types alone are just syntactic validity.

questions.q: Define domain, relation, tuple, attribute and active domain.
questions.a:
- Domain: a set of possible values, not necessarily of a simple data type.
- Relation: a subset of a Cartesian product of domains.
- Tuple: a single element of the relation.
- Attribute: an element of a tuple; several attributes may share a domain.
- Active domain: the values currently present in the relation.

questions.q: List the properties of a relation in the relational model, and explain three ways SQL tables differ from them.
questions.a:
Relational model: relations and attributes are identified by name; values are atomic; there is no NULL; no two tuples are equal; the order of tuples and of attributes is irrelevant.
SQL differs:
- Duplicates: rows may repeat unless DISTINCT (or UNION / EXCEPT instead of UNION ALL / EXCEPT ALL) removes them.
- Order: rows come out in an order (ORDER BY, GROUP BY, indexes).
- NULLs: SQL has NULLs, outer joins and three-valued logic.
questions.hint: Duplicates, order, missing values.

questions.q: STUDENTS(SSN, FName, LName) = {(1342, Bob, Smith), (2984, Alice, Carpenter), (981, John, McAlister), (345, Bob, Lorentz), (654, John, McAlister)}. Give the results of R2 = πFName,LName(STUDENTS) and R4 = πFName,LName(σSSN<1000(STUDENTS)). Why is R3 = σSSN<1000(πFName,LName(STUDENTS)) not a valid expression?
questions.a:
R2 = {(Bob, Smith), (Alice, Carpenter), (John, McAlister), (Bob, Lorentz)}: four tuples, because projection removes the duplicate John McAlister.
R4: the selection keeps SSN 981, 345, 654; projecting gives {(John, McAlister), (Bob, Lorentz)}: two tuples.
R3 is invalid because the projection drops SSN, so the selection predicate SSN < 1000 refers to an attribute that no longer exists. The order of operations matters.
questions.hint: Count duplicates after projecting; check which attributes exist after each step.

questions.q: STUDENTS has SSN 1342, 2984, 981, 345, 654; ENROLMENT(SSN, CourseCode) = {(1342, DB12), (1342, CS1), (2000, DB12), (345, DB12)}. How many tuples do the natural join STUDENTS ⨝ ENROLMENT and the theta join STUDENTS ⨝S.SSN<E.SSN ENROLMENT return?
questions.a:
Natural join (on SSN): 1342 matches two enrolments and 345 matches one; 2000 has no student. Result: 3 tuples (Bob Smith DB12, Bob Smith CS1, Bob Lorentz DB12).
Theta join S.SSN < E.SSN, counting enrolment SSNs larger than each student's:
- 1342: only 2000, 1 pair
- 2984: none
- 981: 1342, 1342, 2000, 3 pairs
- 345: 1342, 1342, 2000, 3 pairs
- 654: 1342, 1342, 2000, 3 pairs
Total: 10 tuples.
questions.hint: For the theta join, compare every student with every enrolment row.

questions.q: Using STUDENTS and ENROLMENT from the joins example, what do STUDENTS ⋉ ENROLMENT and STUDENTS ⩥ ENROLMENT return? Write both in terms of basic operations.
questions.a:
STUDENTS ⋉ ENROLMENT = π attr(STUDENTS)(STUDENTS ⨝ ENROLMENT): the students who have an enrolment, {(1342, Bob, Smith), (345, Bob, Lorentz)}.
STUDENTS ⩥ ENROLMENT = STUDENTS \ (STUDENTS ⋉ ENROLMENT): the students without one, {(2984, Alice, Carpenter), (981, John, McAlister), (654, John, McAlister)}.

questions.q: STAFF(SSN, FName, LName) = {(1342, Arkadiusz, Kowalski), (2984, Alice, Carpenter), (981, John, Smith)}. With STUDENTS as before, how many tuples are in STUDENTS ∪ STAFF and in πFName,LName(STUDENTS) \ πFName,LName(STAFF)? What integrity problem does the union reveal?
questions.a:
STUDENTS ∪ STAFF: 5 + 3 tuples with one in common, (2984, Alice, Carpenter), so 7 tuples.
The name difference: the student names are Bob Smith, Alice Carpenter, John McAlister and Bob Lorentz; removing staff names leaves Bob Smith, John McAlister and Bob Lorentz, 3 tuples.
The union is algebraically valid, but SSN 1342 now appears with two different people (Bob Smith and Arkadiusz Kowalski), so SSN no longer identifies a person: the operation output does not respect the integrity of the data.
questions.hint: Union needs compatible schemas, not consistent meaning.

questions.q:
In STUDENTS(SSN, FName, LName, CourseCode) one of five rows has CourseCode = NULL. How many rows do these queries return, and why?
SELECT * FROM STUDENTS WHERE SSN > 1000 OR NOT (SSN > 1000)
SELECT * FROM STUDENTS WHERE CourseCode > 300 OR NOT (CourseCode > 300)
questions.a:
The first returns all 5 rows: SSN is never NULL, so the condition is TRUE for every row.
The second returns 4 rows: for the NULL row both comparisons are UNKNOWN, and UNKNOWN OR UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN, so WHERE drops it. A WHERE clause keeps only rows where the condition is TRUE.
questions.hint: What is NOT UNKNOWN?

questions.q: Name three algebraic transformation rules an optimiser can use, and say why selection pushdown matters.
questions.a:
- Selection commutativity and combination: σX(σY(R)) = σY(σX(R)) = σX and Y(R).
- Selection pushdown: σX(R ⨝ S) = σX(R) ⨝ S when X uses only attributes of R.
- Projection cascade and pushdown: πX(πY(R)) = πX(R) iff X ⊆ Y; keep only needed attributes before a join.
- Join commutativity and associativity: reorder joins.
Selection pushdown reduces the number of tuples before the expensive join, which is important for performance.

questions.q: Which relational algebra operation eliminates duplicate tuples as a direct effect of changing the attributes?
questions.hint: Dropping columns can make two different rows identical.
questions.r: Slide 7: projection keeps only the listed attributes, so formerly different tuples can coincide; since a relation has no duplicates, they collapse into one. Selection keeps whole tuples, rename only renames, and a product combines.

questions.q: Which requirement must hold before two relations can be combined with a Cartesian product?
o: Their attribute names must be distinct
They must share at least one attribute
Both must have the same number of tuples
questions.hint: The result has every attribute of both inputs side by side.
questions.r: Slide 7: the product creates all combinations and keeps all attributes, so names must be unambiguous; otherwise rename (ρ) first. Union and difference need compatible schemas; a natural join needs shared attributes.

questions.q: What does UNKNOWN AND FALSE evaluate to in SQL's three-valued logic?
questions.hint: If one side of AND is FALSE, does the other side matter?
questions.r: Slide 18: FALSE AND anything is FALSE, including UNKNOWN. In contrast UNKNOWN AND TRUE is UNKNOWN, and TRUE OR anything is TRUE.

questions.q: Which expression is equal to R ∩ S?
questions.hint: Remove from R everything that is not in S.
questions.r: Slide 11: R \ S is the part of R outside S; removing it from R leaves exactly the tuples in both. Equivalently S \ (S \ R).

questions.q: Why does storing U(SSN, FName, LName, CourseCode, CourseName, FinalGrade) in one table cause anomalies? Describe the update, insert and delete anomaly.
questions.a:
U stores several independent facts (people, courses, grades) in one relation, so facts repeat and must be kept consistent everywhere; domain constraints cannot enforce that.
- Update: changing a course name must be done in every row of that course, or the copies disagree.
- Insert: a new course cannot be stored until some student has a grade in it.
- Delete: deleting the last grade of a course also deletes the course name.

questions.q: Decompose U(SSN, FName, LName, CourseCode, CourseName, FinalGrade) into relations that each store one fact. Which FDs justify the split?
questions.a:
- R1(SSN, FName, LName) = πSSN,FName,LName(U): people, from SSN → FName, LName
- R2(CourseCode, CourseName) = πCourseCode,CourseName(U): courses, from CourseCode → CourseName
- R3(SSN, CourseCode, FinalGrade) = πSSN,CourseCode,FinalGrade(U): grades, from SSN, CourseCode → FinalGrade

questions.q: R(ABC) = {(a1, b1, c1), (a2, b2, c1)}. Check by joining whether the decompositions into R1(AC), R2(BC) and into R1(AB), R2(AC) are lossless.
questions.a:
R1(AC) = {(a1, c1), (a2, c1)} and R2(BC) = {(b1, c1), (b2, c1)}; joining on C gives (a1, b1, c1), (a1, b2, c1), (a2, b1, c1), (a2, b2, c1): four tuples, two spurious, so the decomposition is lossy.
R1(AB) = {(a1, b1), (a2, b2)} and R2(AC) = {(a1, c1), (a2, c1)}; joining on A gives exactly (a1, b1, c1) and (a2, b2, c1), so it is lossless. The common attribute A determines the attributes of R1.
questions.hint: Join on the common attribute and compare with R.

questions.q: Define a functional dependency X → Y formally. Why must FDs come from the description of reality rather than from the data in the table?
questions.a:
X → Y holds iff for all tuples t1, t2: t1[X] = t2[X] implies t1[Y] = t2[Y].
The current content is only a sample: it can refute a dependency but never prove it, and FDs must hold for every admissible state, even an empty relation. Whether a dependency holds depends on the reality being modelled.

questions.q: State Armstrong's three axioms and the three derived rules.
questions.a:
Axioms:
- Transitivity: X → Y and Y → Z give X → Z
- Augmentation: X → Y gives XZ → YZ
- Reflexivity: if Y ⊆ X then X → Y
Derived rules:
- Union: X → Y and X → Z give X → YZ
- Decomposition: X → YZ gives X → Y and X → Z
- Pseudotransitivity: X → Y and YW → Z give XW → Z

questions.q: Classify as trivial, non-trivial or completely non-trivial: (a) SSN, CourseCode → SSN; (b) SSN, CourseCode → FinalGrade; (c) SSN → FName; (d) SSN, CourseCode → SSN, FinalGrade.
questions.a:
- (a) trivial: the right side is a subset of the left side
- (b) completely non-trivial: the sides share no attribute
- (c) completely non-trivial
- (d) non-trivial but not completely non-trivial: SSN appears on both sides

questions.q: Which functional dependency is trivial?
questions.hint: A trivial FD says nothing new: the right side is already in the left side.
questions.r: Slide 16: X → Y is trivial when Y ⊆ X. SSN is part of {SSN, CourseCode}, so it holds in every relation regardless of the data. The other three carry real information.

questions.q: X → Y and YW → Z together give XW → Z. What is this rule called?
questions.hint: It looks like transitivity with something extra added on the left.
questions.r: Slide 17: pseudotransitivity is a derived rule (augment X → Y with W, then apply transitivity). Augmentation adds the same attributes to both sides; decomposition splits a right side; reflexivity gives trivial FDs.

questions.q: What two properties should a decomposition of R into R1 and R2 have, according to the lecture?
o: Lossless join, and if possible dependency preservation
Equal numbers of attributes in both resulting relations
No shared attributes, and the same primary key in both
Every relation in BCNF, even if the join adds tuples
questions.hint: One property is a must, the other is desirable.
questions.r: Slide 8: a good decomposition must be lossless (R1 ⨝ R2 = R) and should preserve functional dependencies when possible. Shared attributes are needed for the join to work.

questions.q: For R(ABCDE, A → BC, C → D, DA → E), compute A+ step by step. Is A a candidate key? Does C → E hold?
questions.a:
Start {A}. A → BC gives {A, B, C}. C → D gives {A, B, C, D}. DA → E gives {A, B, C, D, E}.
A+ = ABCDE, so A is a superkey; a single attribute is minimal, so A is a candidate key.
C+ = {C, D}: E is not in it (DA → E needs A), so C → E does not hold.
questions.hint: Keep applying FDs whose left side is already in the result.

questions.q: Find all candidate keys and the prime and non-prime attributes of R(ABCD, A → B, BC → D, D → C).
questions.a:
Mandatory attributes (on no right side): A. A+ = AB, not everything.
Add one attribute: AC+ = ABCD (A → B, BC → D); AD+ = ABCD (A → B, D → C); AB+ = AB.
Both AC and AD are minimal (A+, C+ and D+ are not everything).
Candidate keys: AC and AD. Prime: A, C, D. Non-prime: B.
questions.hint: Start from the attributes that never appear on a right-hand side.

questions.q: Find all candidate keys of R(ABCDE, A → B, C → D, BC → E, DE → C).
questions.a:
Mandatory: A, and A+ = AB.
One more attribute: AC+ = ABCDE, so AC is a key. AD+ = ABD, AE+ = ABE, AB+ = AB.
Two more (without C, since supersets of AC are pruned): ADE+ = ADE, then DE → C, then B and E: ABCDE. AD, AE and DE alone fall short, so ADE is minimal.
Candidate keys: AC and ADE. Prime: A, C, D, E. Non-prime: B.
questions.hint: After AC, look for keys that reach C through another FD.

questions.q: Define 2NF, 3NF and BCNF.
questions.a:
- 2NF: in 1NF and every non-prime attribute is fully functionally dependent on every candidate key (no dependence on part of a key).
- 3NF: in 2NF and for every non-trivial X → Y in F+, X is a superkey or Y is prime.
- BCNF: in 3NF and for every non-trivial X → Y in F+, X is a superkey.

questions.q: Is U(SSN, FName, LName, CourseCode, CourseName, FinalGrade; SSN → FName, LName; CourseCode → CourseName; SSN, CourseCode → FinalGrade) in 2NF? And is R(ABC, A → B, B → C) in 3NF?
questions.a:
U: the only candidate key is {SSN, CourseCode}. FName and LName depend on SSN alone, part of the key, so they are partially dependent: U is in 1NF but not 2NF.
R: the key is A (A+ = ABC). Single-attribute key, so 2NF. B → C has a left side that is not a superkey and C is not prime, so R is not in 3NF (transitive dependency A → B → C).

questions.q: R(Student, Course, Instructor; Student, Course → Instructor; Instructor → Course) is decomposed into R1(Instructor, Course) and R2(Instructor, Student). What is the NF of R, R1 and R2? Is the decomposition lossless and dependency preserving?
questions.a:
R: keys {Student, Course} and {Student, Instructor}; all attributes are prime, so R is 3NF. Instructor → Course has a non-superkey left side, so R is not BCNF.
R1(Instructor, Course) with Instructor → Course: BCNF. R2(Instructor, Student) has no non-trivial FD: BCNF.
Lossless: the common attribute Instructor determines all of R1.
Not dependency preserving: Student, Course → Instructor cannot be derived from Instructor → Course alone.

questions.q: R(ABC, A → B, B → C) is decomposed into R1(AC), R2(BC), and alternatively into R1(AB), R2(AC). For each, is it lossless? Is it dependency preserving?
questions.a:
R1(AC), R2(BC): common attribute C; C+ = C determines neither AC nor BC, so it is lossy. F1 = {A → C}, F2 = {B → C}: A → B is lost, so it is not dependency preserving either.
R1(AB), R2(AC): common attribute A determines AB, so it is lossless. F1 = {A → B}, F2 = {A → C}: B → C cannot be derived, so it is not dependency preserving.
questions.hint: Use the common-attribute test for losslessness and F+ = (F1 ∪ F2)+ for preservation.

questions.q: Find a minimal cover of R(ABCDE, A → B, C → D, BC → DE, DE → C, ACD → E, AC → D).
questions.a:
Step 1, single attributes on the right: A → B, C → D, BC → D, BC → E, DE → C, ACD → E, AC → D.
Step 2, extraneous left attributes: BC → D reduces to C → D; AC → D reduces to C → D; ACD → E reduces to AC → E, since D follows from C.
Step 3, redundant FDs: drop the duplicate C → D copies, and AC → E, which follows from A → B and BC → E.
Minimal cover: A → B, C → D, BC → E, DE → C.

questions.q: List the steps of the 3NF synthesis algorithm and what it guarantees.
questions.a:
1. Find a minimal cover G of F.
2. Group FDs with identical left sides.
3. For each group X → Y create a relation with attributes XY.
4. Remove relations whose attributes are contained in another relation.
5. If no relation contains a candidate key of R, add one that does.
Guarantees: lossless, dependency preserving, every relation in 3NF.

questions.q: In 3NF, a non-trivial FD X → Y whose left side X is not a superkey is still allowed when:
o: Y is part of the primary key only
X appears in no other dependency
questions.hint: This is exactly the escape clause that BCNF removes.
questions.r: Slide 16: 3NF requires for every non-trivial X → Y that X is a superkey or Y is prime (belongs to some candidate key, not only the primary key). BCNF drops the second option.

questions.q: Which three properties of the attribute-set closure X+ are listed in the lecture?
questions.hint: X ⊆ X+, a bigger set gives a bigger closure, and closing twice changes nothing.
questions.r: Slide 5: X ⊆ X+ (extensivity), X ⊆ Y ⇒ X+ ⊆ Y+ (monotonicity), (X+)+ = X+ (idempotence). Reflexivity, augmentation and transitivity are Armstrong's axioms for FDs.

questions.q: An attribute is prime when it:
o: belongs to at least one candidate key
belongs to the chosen primary key
appears on the left of some dependency
is determined by every candidate key
questions.hint: Any candidate key counts, not only the one chosen as primary.
questions.r: Slide 11: a prime attribute belongs to at least one candidate key; a non-prime attribute belongs to none. The choice of primary key does not matter.

questions.q: Given R(X, F), how do you check whether a set of attributes Z is a superkey?
o: Compute Z+ and check that it equals all attributes X
Check that Z appears on the left of every dependency
Check that no attribute of Z appears on a right side
Compute F+ and check that Z → Z is listed in it
questions.hint: A superkey determines every attribute of the relation.
questions.r: Slide 8: Z is a superkey iff Z+ = X. A candidate key is a superkey that is minimal. Z → Z is trivial and holds for any Z.

questions.q: Synthesise a 3NF schema for R(ABCDE, A → B, C → D, BC → DE, DE → C, AC → D). Show the minimal cover, the relations, and how losslessness is ensured.
questions.a:
Minimal cover: A → B, C → D, BC → E, DE → C.
One relation per left side: R1(AB, A → B), R2(CD, C → D), R3(BCE, BC → E), R4(CDE, DE → C, C → D). R2 is contained in R4 and is dropped.
Candidate keys of R: AC and ADE. None of R1, R3, R4 contains one, so add R5(AC).
Result: R1(AB), R3(BCE), R4(CDE), R5(AC): lossless and dependency preserving.

questions.q: In the synthesised schema R1(AB), R3(BCE), R4(CDE, DE → C, C → D), R5(AC), what is the normal form of each relation? Justify R4.
questions.a:
R1(AB, A → B): BCNF. R3(BCE, BC → E): BCNF, BC is a key. R5(AC): BCNF, no non-trivial FD.
R4: keys DE (DE+ = CDE) and CE (CE+ = CDE). C → D has a left side that is not a superkey, so R4 is not BCNF; D is prime (in key DE), so R4 is in 3NF.

questions.q: The iterative procedure on the same relation gives R1(AB, A → B), R2(CD, C → D), R3(ACE, AC → E). Compare it with the synthesis result.
questions.a:
All three iterative relations are in BCNF, a stronger normal form than synthesis reaches for R4(CDE).
But DE → C no longer fits inside any relation and cannot be derived from A → B, C → D, AC → E, so the iterative result is not dependency preserving.
Synthesis keeps every dependency at the price of one relation (R4) being only 3NF.

questions.q: A relation in 1NF has only single-attribute candidate keys. What can you conclude immediately?
questions.hint: A partial dependency needs a key with at least two attributes.
questions.r: Slide 8: with single-attribute keys no attribute can depend on part of a key, so 2NF holds. 3NF can still fail through a transitive dependency such as A → B → C.

questions.q: A relation in 3NF has exactly one candidate key. Which normal form does it reach?
questions.hint: The 3NF escape clause needs a prime attribute from another key.
questions.r: Slide 8: with exactly one candidate key, a 3NF relation is also in BCNF.

questions.q: Every attribute of a 1NF relation is prime. Which normal form is guaranteed?
questions.hint: 3NF allows X → Y with a non-key X when Y is prime.
questions.r: Slide 8: if all attributes are prime, every right side is prime, so the 3NF condition always holds. BCNF is not guaranteed (Student, Course, Instructor is the classic case).
